title: I'm nobody
hookLine: I'm nobody! who are you? are you nobody too?
tomorrow: what kind of winter light did Dickinson say could hurt?

cards: Follower counts, view counts, the little number under every post. Dickinson wrote a poem that could be answering all of them. "I'm nobody! Who are you? Are you nobody, too?"
Then there's a pair of us, she whispers; don't tell. "How dreary to be somebody!" Being somebody, she says, is like a frog croaking its own name all day long to an admiring bog.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: A SWEET, HIDDEN LIFE.
teach.b: People who love this poem read it two ways. One side hears it straight: a woman who chose a hidden life and found it sweet.
Dickinson spent much of her life at home and kept many of her poems in booklets she sewed by hand.
In this reading, being nobody is freedom: no performance, no audience to feed, and a secret friendship of two nobodies while somebody croaks to the bog.

teach.h: THE OTHER: AN ACHE UNDER THE JOKE.
teach.b: The other side hears an ache under the joke.
This is the same poet who sent poems to a magazine writer, Thomas Wentworth Higginson, and asked him if her verse was alive. That's not someone who wanted no readers.

In this reading, nobody is a brave face on being unseen. Both sides can point to the text. The exclamation marks sound like delight; the don't tell sounds like someone who knows the world might laugh.
What both readings share is the teaching itself. Dickinson finds company in being nobody: who are you? are you nobody, too?
Being unknown isn't the same as being alone.
And worth isn't measured by the size of the bog that's listening.

how: Some readers of Dickinson share this poem as a quiet answer to the pressure to be seen; teachers pair it with her letters to Higginson to show both readings.

o: she sent poems to a magazine writer and asked if her verse was alive; she wanted readers.
she disliked everyone, and the poem is an insult to the reader.

games.why: that's the strongest case for the ache. the poem holds both: delight in a hidden pair, and a poet who also hoped to be read.

practice: Sit the way an ordinary person sits in a crowd: shoulders loose, nobody watching, nothing to prove. Let your face rest. For the length of the sit, be nobody, and know that somewhere a stranger is nobody right alongside you.

wordCard.voice: I'm nobody: Dickinson's glad whisper to a stranger, are you nobody, too? Being unknown, in her poem, is a kind of company, not a lack.
